clue.text: Enraged sopranos dismissing a patron

indicators.note: something enraged is wild and out of control, so its letters are thrown into a new order
to dismiss is to send away, so the named letter is removed from the word before it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; this letter is the one removed

explanation.surface: A group of furious opera singers send their wealthy backer packing.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one A out of SOPRANOS to leave SOPRNOS, then rearrange those seven letters to get SPONSOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A patron funds and supports an artist or event, which is exactly what a backer who sponsors does.

clue.text: Sheep turned to climb — grumble about that?

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: to sulk is to grumble moodily; it forms the outside

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: milk that has turned has gone off

explanation.surface: A farmer complains about a sheep that went off and climbed somewhere it shouldn't.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' is not a reversal signal here: it means gone sour, as milk does; 'to climb' does the reversing, and 'that' points back to the climbed piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Suffolk is a well-known English breed of sheep with a black face, named after its home county.

clue.text: Cat to strike, leaving quietly

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so that letter goes out of the word

parts.note: to pounce is to strike suddenly, as a cat does
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: A cat about to pounce slips away silently instead.
explanation.walkthrough: POUNCE loses its P to give OUNCE; the surface cleverly makes the cat the striker, while the cat is actually the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ounce is an old name for the snow leopard, a big wild cat of Central Asian mountains.

clue.text: Good sort introducing vespers no good as writer

indicators.note: to introduce is to bring forward next, so what follows is placed straight after

parts.note: a saint, abbreviated ST, is a very good person

indicators.note: 'no' says the following item is absent, so its letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: vespers is the evening church service, evensong
G is a standard abbreviation for good; it is removed

explanation.surface: A kindly person brings evening prayers that turn out to be no good as a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: ST, a saint, comes first; EVENSONG loses its G to give EVENSON, and together they spell STEVENSON.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson, Scottish author of Treasure Island and Kidnapped, is a famous novelist.

clue.text: Stylish liturgy endlessly supported by unknowns

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
in a down entry, being supported means having something placed underneath

parts.note: a rite is a set form of worship, a liturgy
Z and Y are algebra's usual unknowns

explanation.surface: A fashionable church service is kept going by people nobody has heard of.
explanation.walkthrough: RITE loses its last letter, and the unknowns sit beneath it because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritzy means luxurious and smart, from the opulent Ritz hotels, so it is a synonym for stylish.

clue.text: Inclination to avoid parking in transport

indicators.note: avoiding something means keeping it out, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a penchant is a liking or inclination
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A preference for leaving the car at home and using public transport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport' looks like buses and trains, but here it is a verb meaning to delight; PENCHANT minus P gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To transport someone is to carry them away with delight, the same sense as to charm or captivate.

clue.text: Superheat liquid in long river

indicators.note: something liquid flows and has no fixed shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Water heated to extreme temperatures flowing in a great river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liquid' fits the watery surface so well it reads as a noun, but it is the signal to rearrange the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Euphrates flows nearly three thousand kilometres through Turkey, Syria and Iraq, one of western Asia's longest waterways.

clue.text: Boorish, but he avoids collisions

indicators.note: to avoid is to keep away from, so those letters stay out of the word

parts.note: crashes are collisions
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A rude driver who nonetheless never has an accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' looks like the driver, but it is just the two letters taken out of CRASHES.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass means coarse, insensitive and lacking refinement, a close synonym of boorish behaviour.

clue.text: Restrained element breaking away

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: someone away is absent; this is the outer word
tin is a chemical element

explanation.surface: A self-controlled part of a group breaking off on its own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking away' reads as one phrase meaning splitting off, but the two words do separate jobs: 'breaking' is the insertion signal and 'away' supplies the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone abstinent holds back from indulging, especially in alcohol, so they are self-controlled and restrained.

clue.text: Modified material from Harris a king wears

indicators.note: what is worn goes round the wearer, so the outer word clothes the inner ones

parts.note: Harris Tweed is the famous cloth woven in the Outer Hebrides
taken as written
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: An altered fabric from Harris that a monarch puts on.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the king wearing the cloth, but the cryptic reading is the cloth wearing the king: TWEED goes round A and K.
explanation.definitionFit: To tweak something is to adjust it slightly, so tweaked describes something that has been altered.

clue.text: Identify suspect advice in digital feature

parts.note: to finger someone is to identify them as the culprit
a tip is a piece of useful advice

explanation.surface: Spotting dodgy guidance inside some feature of a computer or phone app.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' suggests computers, but it means relating to the digits, the fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: A digit is a finger, so the end of one is literally a part, or feature, of a digit.

clue.text: A key passage

parts.note: taken as written
a key or cay is a low island, as in the Florida Keys

explanation.surface: An important section of a text, or a crucial corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key passage' reads as an important extract, but the key is a small island, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: An aisle is a walkway between rows of seats or shelves, so it is a narrow passage.

clue.text: Like Bunter sitting inside to be served?

indicators.note: something sitting inside other words is tucked within them, spanning their letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A greedy schoolboy waiting indoors for his dinner to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters hide in 'tO BE SErved'. Billy Bunter is the famously fat, greedy schoolboy of the old Greyfriars school stories by Frank Richards.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunter was drawn as hugely overweight and always hungry, so being like him means very fat.

clue.text: Standard staff attached to police HQ

indicators.note: being attached to something means joined onto its end, so these sit side by side

parts.note: the Yard is Scotland Yard, London's Metropolitan Police headquarters
a staff is a walking stick

explanation.surface: Regular employees assigned to work at the police headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like personnel, but it is a wooden pole. The stick is attached after the police HQ.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardstick is a measure for comparison, a benchmark, which is what a standard means.

clue.text: Gives up bitter to give sudden impulse

parts.note: to kick a habit is to give it up
tart means sharp or bitter in taste

explanation.surface: A drinker quits bitter beer and suddenly feels a need for something new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' tempts as the British beer, but it is the taste adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To kick-start something is to set it going with a burst of energy, like starting a motorcycle with a kick.

clue.text: Come in with fish and chips

indicators.note: 'with' means alongside, so the two pieces are simply put together

parts.note: a carp is a freshwater fish
to enter is to come in

explanation.surface: An invitation to step inside for a British fish-and-chips supper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish and chips' is the famous British takeaway, but 'and' only joins, and Chips is the traditional nickname for a carpenter, especially a ship's carpenter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chips is old slang, especially naval, for a woodworker, from the wood chips such a tradesman produces.

clue.text: Absurd drama done for stars

indicators.note: something absurd makes no sense, so these letters must be set in a sensible order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A ridiculous play put on for its celebrity actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' looks like the famous cast, but it means a constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: Andromeda is a constellation of the northern sky, a named group of stars, also home to a famous galaxy.

clue.text: Devotee in China quelling resistance

indicators.note: to quell is to suppress or put down, so that letter is wiped out

parts.note: in cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, a friend
R is the physics symbol for electrical resistance; it is removed

explanation.surface: A loyal follower in China helping to crush a rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country but is cockney rhyming slang, where china plate rhymes with mate.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiend can be an enthusiast or addict, as in a fitness fiend, so it fits a keen follower.

clue.text: Inactive uranium fast producing gas

parts.note: a flat market or mood is inactive and sluggish
U is the chemical symbol for uranium
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: Inert uranium rapidly giving off gas in a nuclear reaction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' reads as quickly, but it is a period of abstaining from food.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatulent means suffering from wind in the gut, literally generating intestinal gas.

clue.text: Nobleman in love shed clothes

indicators.note: to clothe something is to cover it all round, so one word wraps another

parts.note: a barn is a farm shed; it forms the outside
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: An aristocrat in love who has stripped off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed clothes' looks like undressing, but 'shed' is a farm building and 'clothes' is a verb, covering O.
explanation.definitionFit: A baron is a member of the peerage, the lowest rank of British nobility.

clue.text: The point of retirement?

parts.note: surface reading: the purpose of stopping work, or the age when one leaves a career
setter's reading: retiring in the sense of going up for the night, so the hour at which it happens

explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' looks like purpose and 'retirement' like leaving work, but 'point' is a moment in time and to retire is to go to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To retire for the night means heading upstairs to sleep, and the usual hour for doing that is the answer.

clue.text: Sad secret out for French thinker

indicators.note: 'out' can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters are put into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy confidence gets leaked about a philosopher from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' reads as revealed, which suits a secret, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: René Descartes was the seventeenth-century French philosopher of 'I think, therefore I am'.

clue.text: Poet and writer in ship on turning turtle

indicators.note: 'in' places one thing inside another, so it sits within the outer letters

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship; it forms the outside
a pen is a writing instrument

indicators.note: a boat turning turtle capsizes and ends upside down, so the word is flipped

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A poet and an author on board a vessel that capsizes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning turtle' tempts you to flip the whole thing, but it acts only on 'on', which is the short word meaning regarding, as in a memo heading.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan author of The Faerie Queene, a major English poet.

clue.text: Daughter leaves black grain in dish

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
a ream is a quantity of paper, made of leaves or sheets
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black
oat is a cereal grain

explanation.surface: A girl walks away from a burnt cereal in a bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb meaning departs, but it is the noun for sheets of paper; 'dish' is slang for a gorgeous person.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish is informal for a very attractive person, and so is a dreamboat; both are slang compliments.

clue.text: Notices Kelvin tucking into chocolate bar

indicators.note: tucking into something means slipping inside it, so a letter goes within a word

parts.note: a Mars bar is a well-known chocolate bar; it forms the outside
K is the symbol for the kelvin temperature unit

explanation.surface: Someone spots a man called Kelvin eating a chocolate bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' reads as eating, but it means going inside: K slips into MARS.
explanation.definitionFit: To mark something can mean to notice or observe it, as in 'mark my words'.

clue.text: Saw things in Société Ethnologique?

indicators.note: 'in' says the letters lie inside the words that follow, spanning them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second, ignoring the accent

explanation.surface: Things seen at a French anthropology society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is the cutting tool; the accent on the É is ignored, as accents always are in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw cuts with a row of sharp points along its blade, which are called its teeth.

clue.text: United by wise tradition

indicators.note: 'by' means next to, so the pieces are placed side by side

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names
sage means wise

explanation.surface: People brought together by a long-held, wise custom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United' reads as a verb but here is the abbreviation U, as in Man U.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is established custom or practice, a habit handed down, so it can mean tradition.

clue.text: Fabulous writer misinterpreted as Poe

indicators.note: something misinterpreted is read the wrong way, so the letters come out in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wonderful author who has been wrongly taken for Edgar Allan Poe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' looks like praise, but it means 'of fables'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek storyteller credited with the fables, so he is literally a writer of fables.

clue.text: Football club's at home? They're regularly sent away

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

indicators.note: sending away at regular intervals throws out every other letter, keeping the rest

parts.note: the first, third and fifth characters survive

explanation.surface: A football team playing a home game whose players keep getting sent off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent away' sounds like red cards, but with 'regularly' it tells you to drop every other letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Inter Milan, usually called just Inter, is a famous Italian football team based in Milan.

clue.text: Teams beginning to enjoy second drinks break

parts.note: football and cricket teams have eleven players, so they are elevens

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: only the opening letter is used
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Two sides start to enjoy a second pause for refreshments mid-match.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is a British mid-morning break for tea or coffee and a snack, taken around eleven o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a short pause in the morning for a cup of tea or coffee, so a pause for beverages.

clue.text: Large area of capital's a Parisian street heading west

indicators.note: in an across entry, travelling west means right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: capital means first-rate, A or A1
the apostrophe-s stands for 'is'
taken as written
rue is French for street

explanation.surface: A big district of the French capital is a westbound road in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts as Paris, but it means excellent, A as in A1. A IS A RUE then runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurasia is the combined landmass of Europe and Asia, the largest continental expanse on Earth.

clue.text: Passionate urge for Shakespeare's Percy

parts.note: hot means passionate or fiery
to spur is to urge on

explanation.surface: A fiery yearning to play the part of Shakespeare's Percy.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are plain synonyms; the knowledge needed is that Harry Percy is the hot-headed rebel in Henry IV Part 1.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Percy appears in Henry IV Part 1 under his nickname, earned for his rash, fiery temperament.
